doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Einstein's Red/Blue Universe at Carnegie Hall
summary: Her first piece for symphony orchestra with brass moving in the balconies, and the nervous premiere.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: You also had a piece performed at Carnegie Hall, isn’t that right?

Yeah. That was like a further incarnation of some of that NASA work. Basically that was a piece called “Einstein’s Red/Blue Universe,” and it was played by The American Composers Orchestra, a very fine new music orchestra in New York, conducted by Dennis Russell Davies, and it was my first piece for full symphony orchestra and jazz musicians, and sound surround brass choirs in the Carnegie Hall balconies. It was the funniest thing. We had — in order to maximize the use of the musicians there are points in the score where the brass section has to leave the stage and get up to the balcony in the Carnegie Hall. And that’s pretty precipitous up there by the way. They had to take the elevator to get up there in the middle of the piece.
You had to write the time into the piece for how fast the elevator is going up.

Yup, yup. And then there were also some very carefully orchestrated movement aspects in the piece for the brass sections and woodwind sections in the orchestra. Movement, almost these doppler like movement effects, is very much a part of my kind of intuitive playing style. And over the years, through working with dancers and things, I got interested in orchestrating it, trying to notate it so other musicians, actually whole sections of instruments, could sort of use my original impulse and also move their horns in this doppleresque kind of way to create these timbre shifts. So if you can imagine whole trumpet, trombone and brass sections standing up with bells in the air, and turning 180 and 360° in different directions and different speeds, in unison, to create these kind of spherical soundscapes I guess you could call it. And it’s been a passion of mine, an interest. It came all about from working at NASA. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
Did the people in the orchestra, like how did they handle that?
This is a tremendous new music. There’s nothing these guys can’t do.
Yeah. And they were very generous with their time and their creativity, and they did it.
Tell me, were you really nervous with that premier?

Oh sure. Are you kidding? I mean I’ve stood in front of an orchestra as the soloist, you know like in a classical sense, but with all these other things going on, there’s actually a danger element in this music. I had a choreographer friend come in, just to help teach the brass players how to move and play at the same time without getting dizzy, how not to hyperventilate. This is a new, new technique you know.
God forbid one of them went the wrong way too.
Naa, these were pros, these were professionals.
And were you playing also in this piece?
Oh yeah, yeah. I was like the featured soloist with the improvising jazz musicians, who were still inside the orchestra, but toward the front.
